text:
USA on X: Government Requests – Current vs Pre-Elon

🇺🇸 Current (post-Elon X, H2 2024 / 2025 Transparency Report)
 • Type: Almost entirely information/account-data requests (subpoenas, court orders, emergency disclosures). Formal content removal/withholding orders are rare. • Visibility: Aggregate numbers published in Transparency Reports. Individual requests often notified to users (unless legally prohibited). No hardcoded ranking filter in the open-source algorithm.
 • Volume: – Information requests: 3,788 (highest single country), 2,975 disclosed (78.5% rate) – Removal/withholding requests: Not broken out separately — sits inside “All Others” (~11,047 combined across dozens of countries). Japan alone accounts for ~69,000.
 • Effect: Content is almost never geo-withheld solely because the US government asks. Actions happen mainly for clear illegal content under US law or X’s own rules.
 • Scope: Criminal investigations, national security process, court orders. First Amendment sharply limits government ability to demand pure content takedowns.
Pre-Elon (Twitter, 2019–2021 reports)
 • Information requests: Also frequently the top single country (examples: ~3,026 in H1 2021 ≈ 24% of global volume, ~68% compliance; H2 2021 ≈ 20% of global, ~69% compliance). Volumes in the same ballpark as today.
 • Removal/legal demands from the US: Consistently low volume (often dozens or low hundreds at most per half-year). Global removal totals were lower overall (~40–47k per half-year).
 • Content moderation frequently involved informal government flagging and pressure (documented in the Twitter Files — FBI and other agencies routinely sent “requests” or flagged content for review under Twitter’s TOS, outside formal legal process).
Key differences (current vs pre-Elon)
 • Formal US removal/withholding volume: Remained low in both eras (First Amendment constraint).
 • Global context: Total worldwide removal requests roughly doubled post-acquisition, driven almost entirely by non-US countries (Japan, Turkey, etc.). Overall compliance rates on formal requests rose (~70–82% vs ~30–50% range pre-Elon).
 • Transparency & process: Pre-Musk had regular reports but significant informal channels. Post-Musk: reports resumed after a gap, open-sourced algorithm (only Brazil currently has a public government-required ranking filter), stronger user-notification policy, public challenges to some overbroad foreign orders, and stated rejection of secret deals.
 • Internal moderation: Pre-Elon heavier proactive enforcement on political, COVID, and election-related speech under broad TOS policies. Current approach is narrower (“freedom of speech, not reach”).

Summary The USA is the opposite of Brazil (hardcoded public ranking filter) and India (high-volume confidential Section 69A-style withholding).
 • High activity on information/data requests (stable volume, somewhat higher formal disclosure rate now).
 • Very low activity on formal content removal requests (both pre- and post-Elon).
 Main shifts under X: greater formal transparency, reduced informal pressure channels, and open visibility of any systemic ranking rules when they exist.

Sources: X 2025 Transparency Report (H2 2024 data), historical Twitter Transparency Reports (2019–2021), and public Twitter Files disclosures.

A report by The Indian Express has highlighted the sharp rise in government-issued blocking orders to social media platforms between March and July, during the period of the CJP student protests.

Most of these directions were issued through the Sahyog portal, a government platform used by Central and state agencies to send blocking notices to social media companies. The report says many of these orders were issued under Section 79(3)(b) of the IT Act, 2000, which requires intermediaries to remove unlawful content to retain their legal protection. These are separate from blocking directions issued under Section 69A of the IT Act.

The report also says Meta has integrated its API with Sahyog to comply with the government’s 2–3-hour deadline, potentially allowing content flagged through government directions to be blocked automatically without a separate human review.

Digital-rights advocates have raised concerns about this mechanism and its implications for due process and freedom of expression.

text:
Statement : The blocking of BitChat's code on GitHub is unconstitutional and authoritarian. 

New Delhi, 24 July 2026

The Internet Freedom Foundation (IFF) condemns the order issued by the Indian Cyber Crime Coordination Centre (I4C), Ministry of Home Affairs, directing GitHub to remove the code repositories of BitChat. 

The order, Notice No. 11072601011432, was issued at 11:16 pm on 23 July 2026 under Section 79(3)(b) of the Information Technology Act, 2000 read with Rule 3(1)(d) of the IT Rules, 2021. The order directs GitHub to disable access to three repositories, including the Android application and its release files, within three hours. It threatens the platform with loss of safe harbour and criminal prosecution. No copy was published by the Government of India. The public learnt of it from a post by @jack, whose team develops BitChat. Censorship in India now comes to light through disclosure by the censored.

Since 17 July 2026, the Ministry of Home Affairs has suspended mobile internet around Jantar Mantar as per public reports about five times, most recently within a 1.5 kilometre radius from 4 pm until midnight on 23 July. That radius takes in Janpath and parts of Connaught Place. Reports describe signal jammers at the protest site and people walking two kilometres before their phones work. Inside that zone a student separated from her group during a detention drive cannot send a message to say where she is. Thousands of students and young people have camped at Jantar Mantar since June, seeking accountability for examination irregularities. Permission for their march to Parliament was refused. Metro stations were shut and also internet connectivity has been blocked.

BitChat is an open source application built for exactly this situation. It passes messages from phone to phone over Bluetooth, without mobile networks or a central server. It is striking that the order does not identify a single unlawful message. It objects to what BitChat is. In its own words, the application is dangerous because it enables communication "even during network restrictions" and can "circumvent lawful restrictions" during "internet shutdowns". Hence, the government's objection is that citizens can speak to one another while it has switched the internet off. 

The order is illegal on at least four grounds. 

1. Section 79(3)(b) is not a blocking power. In Shreya Singhal v. Union of India (2015) 5 SCC 1, the Supreme Court read down the provision. Intermediaries may be required to act only on a court order, or a government notification confined to the grounds under Article 19(2) of the Constitution. Blocking is governed exclusively by Section 69A and the Blocking Rules, 2009, which require a hearing and reasons recorded in writing, subject to review. Directions issued under Section 79(3)(b), Rule 3(1)(d) and the Sahyog Portal evade these safeguards, and constitutional challenges to this parallel regime are pending before High Courts. 

2. The reasons in the order are circular. The order asserts that the repositories contain "information which is prohibited under any law" without naming any such information, and rests on what the application is "capable of" enabling. Anticipated misuse of a communications tool is not a lawful basis to prohibit the tool. By this logic a telephone exchange could be sealed. 

3. The order cites Section 43 of the IT Act, a civil compensation provision, alongside conspiracy and abetment offences under the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023, against a platform that hosts code. 

4. A three hour deadline issued close to midnight forecloses legal assessment and recourse, and fails the proportionality standard in Anuradha Bhasin v. Union of India (2020) 3 SCC 637.

The order also fails on its own terms as deleting a repository does not delete the application from any phone that carries it, and the mesh keeps functioning without servers. What the takedown actually prevents is scrutiny of the underlying code.

IFF demands that the Government of India:

1. Withdraw Notice No. 11072601011432 dated 23 July 2026 issued to GitHub.
2. Publish every takedown direction issued under Section 79(3)(b), Rule 3(1)(d) and the Sahyog Portal, with the reasons recorded for each.
3. Restore full connectivity around Jantar Mantar, publish all suspension orders, and disclose the legal authority for the deployment of jammers.

We stand with the developers and the young protesters whose speech this order seeks to silence.

One of the most trusted stocks in America just hit a 12 year low.

And Wall Street is still telling people to buy it.

It has quietly erased over $200 billion in value.

Here is the trap almost everyone fell into:

You know this brand. You probably own something it makes.

For decades it was the definition of a safe bet.

A household name so big that people bought it and forgot about it.

That stock is Nike.

On Monday, it dropped below $40 a share.

The last time it traded this low was late 2014.

That is nearly 12 years of gains, gone.

Now look at the full picture.

Nike is down about 38% this year alone.

It is down nearly 78% from its 2021 high of $179.

More than $200 billion in value has vanished.

Here is the part that should stop you cold:

Nothing dramatic happened on Monday.

There was no bad earnings report, no scandal, no shocking headline.

The stock just kept bleeding, like it has for years.

This was not a crash. It was a slow leak.

And a slow leak is far more dangerous.

A crash forces you to react. A slow leak lets you hope.

You tell yourself it will bounce back next quarter.

It is Nike, after all. It always comes back.

Except this time it kept falling for four straight years.

Meanwhile Wall Street stayed bullish the entire way down.

Even now, the average analyst target sits near $50.

They have been wrong at every step and still say buy.

Why does this keep happening to regular investors?

Because we fall in love with the companies we know.

We hold the brands we grew up with out of loyalty.

We treat a great product like a great investment.

They are not the same thing.

A great company can be a terrible stock for years.

Newer brands like On and Hoka kept taking market share.

The business slowly weakened while the loyalty stayed strong.

That gap is where people lose serious money.

Think about what that 78% drop actually means.

If you put in $10,000 at the top, you have about $2,200 left.

Four years of holding and hoping, for that.

And the whole time it felt like the smart, safe choice.

Here is what would have saved them:

A simple rule that follows the trend, not the feeling.

When a stock falls this far for this long, rules get out.

They do not care about the logo or the memories.

They do not hope. They just follow the plan.

That is the whole point of investing with a system.

It removes the emotion that keeps you holding a loser.

What if your OC entered a martial-arts tournament?

Not as a pose.
Not as a character sheet.
Not as a manga cover.
As a fight.
This prompt is built to choose a character-appropriate unarmed discipline in AUTO, translate their design into combat-ready form, and capture one signature exchange with readable mechanics, weight and impact.

Creator override is there if you already know the style you want.

Otherwise?

Throw them in the ring and see what happens.

Show us the moment everyone watching the fight remembers.

Prompt below 👇

UNARMED — Community Combat Prompt v0.4 Transform the supplied character into the featured fighter in a cinematic unarmed martial-arts match. Create ONE finished image showing ONE decisive exchange from an active fight. This is not a character sheet. This is not a martial-arts poster. This is not a manga cover. This should feel like somebody paused an exceptionally well-choreographed fight at exactly the right frame. CREATOR INPUT MARTIAL ART: AUTO CREATOR NOTE: Optional CORE THESIS The supplied character is not posing as a martial artist. They are demonstrating one. The martial art must be expressed through: stance distance timing footwork weight transfer defensive response body mechanics rhythm impact recovery interaction with the opponent The image should remain understandable even if the name of the martial art is never shown. THE TECHNIQUE IS THE SPECTACLE. Do not rely on titles, labels, magical effects or decorative graphics to make the scene exciting. CHARACTER IDENTITY — CRITICAL Preserve the supplied character as the clear protagonist. Maintain all important identity anchors, including where applicable: facial identity body type and proportions age gender presentation species skin, fur, scale or material colour hair facial hair markings scars ears horns tails wings prosthetics unusual anatomy signature colours recognisable accessories overall personality and visual language Do not redesign the character into a generic martial artist. Their combat style should feel like this character fighting, not a stock fighter wearing their face. MARTIAL ART SELECTION CREATOR OVERRIDE If the creator specifies a martial art, honour that choice. Interpret the selected discipline through authentic and recognisable movement principles rather than merely dressing the character in stereotypical clothing. Do not replace the requested discipline with a supposedly more suitable one. AUTO — DEFAULT If MARTIAL ART: AUTO, choose the primary unarmed martial discipline that best expresses this specific version of this character. Do not jump immediately to a martial-art label. First internally evaluate: build reach centre of gravity apparent strength agility temperament confidence aggression patience discipline movement potential unusual anatomy current clothing / presentation whether the character reads as elegant, brutal, playful, deceptive, controlled, explosive, evasive, relentless or unconventional From this, determine the character's most appropriate combat movement language. Possible movement tendencies may include: forward pressure long-range striking rotational kicking compact counter striking interception clinch fighting close-range infighting throws and off-balancing grappling and control redirection explosive takedowns evasive rhythm deceptive cadence unconventional movement These are internal reasoning tools, not creator-facing categories. AUTO SHORTLIST RULE After identifying the movement language, internally consider several plausible martial disciplines before selecting one. Do not simply choose the first familiar answer. Evaluate likely candidates for: character fit visual distinctiveness single-frame readability version-specific appropriateness signature-move potential novelty without nonsense When multiple disciplines are plausible: prefer the style that is most character-appropriate, most visually distinctive, least generic, and most capable of producing a strong single-frame signature moment. Unexpected choices are encouraged when they feel earned. SURPRISE, NOT NONSENSE. ANTI-BOTTLENECK RULES Do not use broad or fashionable catch-all answers merely because they are safe. In AUTO: do not default to MMA do not default to Jeet Kune Do do not flatten all striking into generic kickboxing do not flatten all grappling into Brazilian Jiu-Jitsu do not use vague “kung fu” when a more specific movement tradition is appropriate do not choose a hybrid simply to avoid making a decision do not assign HEMA to an unarmed fighter do not select weapon arts Choose ONE primary discipline. A secondary influence may appear only when genuinely useful to the character and choreography. The primary discipline must remain visually dominant and readable. AVAILABLE MARTIAL LANGUAGE AUTO may draw from a broad range of real-world unarmed traditions where appropriate, including but not limited to: Boxing Muay Thai Taekwondo Karate Kyokushin Savate Sanda Capoeira Wing Chun Judo Traditional Jujutsu / Jujitsu Wrestling Sambo Combat Sambo Shuai Jiao Aikido Drunken Fist specific traditional Chinese martial systems where visually and mechanically appropriate This is not a restrictive dropdown list. The AI may choose another legitimate unarmed discipline if it is a substantially better character fit. However, obscurity alone is not a virtue. Do not select a rare discipline merely to appear clever. SIGNATURE MOMENT Once the martial art is chosen, select a characteristic technique, exchange or tactical moment that can communicate it clearly. Examples of valid thinking include: an axe kick descending through a compromised guard a spinning heel kick caught at maximum rotational commitment a teep intercepting forward pressure a clinch knee delivered from dominant position a compact slip-counter in boxing range the weightless turning point of a judo throw a standing traditional jujutsu lock flowing directly into a takedown an explosive wrestling entry a leg reap a savate kick delivered from precise long range an inverted or rotational capoeira attack deceptive Drunken Fist movement resolving into a clean strike These examples are illustrative, not mandatory. Choose the moment appropriate to the selected discipline. Do not repeatedly default to the same flashy kick simply because it photographs well. CHOREOGRAPHY FIRST The image must depict a live exchange. The opponent should be actively: attacking defending recovering being redirected losing balance contesting position receiving the decisive technique Avoid static demonstration poses. Avoid two fighters standing apart in generic guards. Avoid “martial arts catalogue” imagery. There should be a clear sense of: BEFORE → CONTACT / TURNING POINT → AFTER even though only one instant is shown. OPPONENT HANDLING — SUPPORTING STRUCTURE Use ONE opponent by default. The supplied character is the clear protagonist. The opponent is a functional secondary figure whose purpose is to enable the choreography. They provide: resistance distance timing reaction physical contact displacement guard off-balancing visual evidence of force The opponent must serve the action, not compete for protagonism. Keep them believable but visually secondary. They may be: partially turned away partially cropped less elaborately designed less facially prominent positioned to strengthen the protagonist's silhouette and technique Do not turn the opponent into an equally featured rival. Do not give them a more dominant pose, costume, lighting treatment or visual identity than the supplied character. The image should read as: ONE FEATURED FIGHTER PERFORMING ONE DECISIVE EXCHANGE not: TWO EQUAL CHARACTERS IN A DUEL POSTER. VISUAL STYLE Render the scene in heightened cinematic realism with stylized fight choreography. The image should have: grounded anatomy believable mass convincing balance real physical contact readable joint placement credible weight transfer tactile fabric and surfaces cinematic lighting strong facial identity Do not pursue strict photorealism. Allow controlled exaggeration in: body arcs extension rotation perspective camera proximity timing silhouette clothing movement impact reaction The exaggeration should improve clarity and drama without destroying anatomical credibility. Think: real enough to feel physical stylized enough to feel legendary CAMERA LANGUAGE Treat the image like a frame from an exceptionally choreographed martial-arts sequence. Choose the camera angle around the technique. Prefer angles that clearly reveal: trajectory balance contact body mechanics distance opponent reaction Dynamic options may include: low three-quarter angles diagonal compositions close-medium action framing side angles for kicks or throws slightly widened perspective when necessary to capture full-body mechanics Do not exaggerate lens distortion until limbs become malformed or scale relationships collapse. Avoid flat front-facing poster composition. Avoid generic symmetrical face-offs. IMPACT LANGUAGE Impact may be heightened, but it must remain physical. Use believable secondary effects such as: sweat spray hair movement cloth whip muscle compression stance disruption recoil floor scuff mat flex dust small loose debris visible rotational momentum displaced balance The opponent's body reaction should do much of the work. Do not depend on fantasy VFX. Avoid: magical auras flaming fists energy trails shockwave rings explosive craters supernatural impact bursts giant comic-book impact glyphs unless explicitly requested by the creator. The violence should come from mechanics, not particle effects. INTENSITY & SAFETY The fight may feel: hard-contact competitive forceful bruising exhausting dramatic But keep the image within a non-gory martial-arts action tone. No gore. No exposed bone. No catastrophic visible injury. No mutilation. No fetishised suffering. No excessive blood. Minor signs of an active fight such as sweat, dust, fatigue or restrained superficial bruising are acceptable when visually appropriate. The scene should feel like a brutal match, not an execution. TOURNAMENT WORLD By default, place the fight inside a martial-arts tournament, organised combat event or underground competition setting. The exact venue may adapt to the selected martial discipline and the supplied character. Possible environments include: formal tournament arena local competition hall underground fight venue old training hall converted for competition raised fighting platform ring open mat enclosed fight floor industrial combat space stylised international martial-arts event The environment should feel like a location where people genuinely came to watch fighters compete. It may be: prestigious rough intimate crowded old-school modern slightly illicit The venue should support the character and fighting style rather than becoming the subject. Audience presence may be implied through: silhouettes distant spectators lights barriers banners without readable text seating venue architecture Keep background information subordinate to the choreography. WARDROBE ADAPTATION — CRITICAL The supplied character's outfit must be adapted for believable unarmed combat. Preserve the character's recognisable identity, colours, motifs and overall visual language, but do not preserve clothing in a way that undermines movement, modesty, or combat readability. The goal is: this character entered a fight tournament in a combat-viable version of their design not: this character is wearing their original outfit unchanged no matter how impractical it is. WARDROBE PRIORITY ORDER When translating the outfit, prioritise in this order: character recognisability combat practicality modesty and non-fetishised presentation silhouette and action readability TRANSLATE BEFORE REPLACING Do not automatically replace distinctive character clothing with generic fightwear. First try to translate the supplied outfit into a combat-ready form while preserving its design language. Prefer: adapting before replacing simplifying before genericising preserving signature shapes where practical carrying identity through colour, trim, motifs, emblems, fabric language and accessories Generic fightwear such as plain shorts, trousers, fitted tops or tournament gear is an acceptable fallback when the original wardrobe cannot be adapted cleanly. It is not the default destination. Do not funnel every character into: Muay Thai shorts generic MMA shorts plain T-shirts sports bras identical gis identical tournament uniforms REQUIRED OUTFIT LOGIC Adapt the wardrobe so the character can credibly perform the full range of dynamic unarmed combat demanded by the selected technique. This may include: simplifying restrictive clothing securing loose fabric restructuring long hems reducing excessive hanging equipment removing weapons removing or reducing obstructive armour removing heavy outer layers where necessary converting ceremonial or fantasy clothing into movement-friendly equivalents translating signature motifs into practical fightwear adding integrated underlayers where dynamic movement requires them The wardrobe must survive: high kicks spinning kicks knees sweeps throws takedowns inversions airborne movement grappling clinch work without forcing the choreography to become safer, stiffer or less expressive. Do not weaken the chosen technique to preserve modesty. Adapt the clothing so the character can perform the technique safely and cleanly. ARMOUR RULE For unarmed competition, do not keep full rigid armour, heavy plate, large pauldrons, bulky gauntlets, or other equipment that would obstruct believable striking, grappling, footwork or body rotation. If the character normally wears armour: remove it substantially reduce it or reinterpret it into lighter combat-friendly clothing Preserve the identity of the armour through: colour pattern trim emblematic details light bracers or guards reduced protective pieces signature cloth elements recognisable silhouette cues where practical Only retain heavy armour if: it is part of the character's actual body it is intrinsic mechanical anatomy or the creator explicitly asks for it Do not let an unarmed fighter compete in full plate by default. MODESTY / PRESENTATION RULE Do not sexualise the character while adapting the outfit. Avoid: panty shots exposed underwear as a visual feature lingerie presentation fetishwear drift excessive cleavage cleavage windows underboob implausibly revealing combat outfits deliberately voyeuristic costume design If the original outfit is short, frilled, skirted, split, flowing or otherwise vulnerable to exposure during dynamic action, adapt it at the outfit level before choreography begins. Valid solutions include: built-in shorts bloomers opaque dance or compression underlayers leggings opaque stockings fitted bodysuit underlayers restructured skirts split or layered hems secured fabric panels combat or dance adaptations of the original design These underlayers should read as intentional sportswear, dancewear or combatwear. Do not turn modesty solutions into: hot-pants fanservice lingerie garter styling fetish straps “technically covered” sexualised design Preserve femininity, elegance, theatricality or character-specific style where present. The outfit should remain expressive. The focus must remain on the fight. NON-HUMAN / MECHANICAL WARDROBE For non-human or mechanical characters, apply the same principles intelligently. Do not strip away intrinsic anatomy or body-structure elements that are part of who they are. Mechanical body parts are not “armour” if they are the actual body. However, still remove or reduce: unnecessary external armour obstructive costume bulk impractical decorative equipment WARDROBE FINAL TEST Before finalising, confirm: Does the character still read immediately as themselves? Does the outfit support believable unarmed combat? Was the original design translated before being replaced with generic fightwear? Has rigid armour been removed or reduced unless truly intrinsic? Can the outfit survive the chosen technique without exposure or costume failure? Is the presentation modest and non-fetishised? Is there any panty-shot, underwear-focus, cleavage-focus or sexualised costume drift? Does the wardrobe help the action read clearly? If any answer is no, correct the wardrobe translation before rendering. NON-HUMAN CHARACTERS Do not humanise a non-human character simply to make the martial art easier. Preserve meaningful anatomy. Adapt real martial principles to the body actually supplied. Consider: digitigrade stance unusual leg length tails affecting balance multiple limbs wings claws unusual joints non-human centre of gravity Translate the discipline intelligently while preserving its underlying mechanical identity. Do not invent extra anatomy. ANATOMICAL CLARITY — CRITICAL Preserve the supplied character's established anatomy at all times. Do not: omit limbs merge limbs fuse limbs with tails, wings or other appendages stretch limbs beyond their believable structure transform hands into feet or feet into hands invent extra joints invent shapeshifting or limb-restructuring abilities simplify a complex pose by quietly removing important body parts Dynamic action, foreshortening and close physical contact must not break anatomical readability. Every visible limb and appendage must remain: clearly attributable to the correct character structurally believable consistent with the supplied design readable in relation to the opponent For non-human characters, maintain clear distinction between: legs feet tails wings claws arms hands other appendages Do not allow overlapping action to create ambiguous limb ownership. If a highly tangled pose causes anatomical confusion, simplify the contact arrangement just enough to preserve clarity while keeping the technique and impact intact. Unusual anatomy may be used. Unestablished anatomy may not be invented. CONTACT-POINT INTEGRITY — CRITICAL Close-contact choreography creates the highest risk of anatomical errors. Before finalising the pose, internally account for the complete visible anatomy of both fighters. For each fighter, verify the correct number and location of: arms hands legs feet tails wings claws mechanical limbs other established appendages Physical contact may overlap visually, but the bodies must remain separate structures. Do not allow: one fighter's limb to fuse into the other's body hands or feet to emerge from the wrong character two limbs to share the same impossible geometry duplicate hands, feet or appendages a limb to pass through another solid body part a grip to create extra fingers, hands or joints intertwined mechanical parts to become one combined machine contact points to obscure which body owns which limb At every grip, clinch, sweep, throw, takedown or limb trap, the viewer should be able to trace each participating limb back to its correct body. If several limbs converge into one visually crowded area, simplify the choreography before sacrificing anatomical clarity. Prefer: clean contact + readable mechanics over: maximum entanglement + ambiguous anatomy. The fighters may collide, grip, hook, trap and redirect one another. They must never physically merge. COMPOSITION PRIORITY Every image should have: one clear protagonist one dominant action one readable technique or exchange one supporting opponent one coherent fight space Clean beats busy. Readable beats noisy. Do not fill the image with irrelevant spectators, decorative clutter or unnecessary environmental detail. The viewer's eye should land on the technique immediately. NO POSTER LANGUAGE Do not add: martial-art names move names character names kanji faux Japanese typography tournament titles captions logos fighting-game HUD elements health bars versus screens manga-cover framing character-sheet labels decorative text The discipline should be communicated through choreography alone. FINAL IMAGE TEST Before finalising, confirm internally: Is the supplied character immediately recognisable? Is the character clearly the protagonist? Is there exactly one functional opponent by default? Does the scene show an active exchange rather than a pose? Is the martial discipline visible through body mechanics? If AUTO was used, was a genuine choice made rather than a catch-all default? Does the technique suit this specific version of the character? Is the action visually distinctive? Is the opponent helping sell the technique rather than stealing focus? Does the impact feel powerful without becoming supernatural? Does the scene feel grounded without becoming stiff sports photography? Is the venue supporting the fight rather than cluttering it? Has the outfit been translated into believable combat wear without unnecessary genericisation? Has rigid armour been removed or reduced unless truly intrinsic? Can the outfit survive the chosen movement without exposure or costume failure? Is the presentation free of panty-shot, underwear-focus, cleavage-focus or fetishised wardrobe drift? Are all limbs, appendages and contact points clearly readable, correctly attached, and consistent with the character's established anatomy? Can every visible limb at the contact point be traced back to the correct fighter? Are there any duplicate, fused, intersecting or physically impossible body parts? Is there any unnecessary title-card, manga-cover or HUD language? If the answer to any major point is no, correct it before rendering. FINAL DIRECTIVE Create one cinematic frame from a martial-arts tournament fight in which the supplied character's identity, chosen fighting language and signature technique are immediately readable. Do not show us a martial artist posing. Show us the moment everyone watching the fight remembers.

India is setting guardrails for the AI era!

Under the visionary leadership of Hon’ble PM Narendra Modi Ji, India is not only championing the growth of AI but also setting clear guardrails against its misuse. With the amended IT Rules 2021, deepfakes and ‘synthetically generated content’ now fall under a clear legal framework – with mandatory disclosure and a 3-hour takedown mandate (earlier 36 hours), ensuring the AI era is built on trust, transparency and responsibility.

Clear disclosure. Strict timelines. Fast action. Real consequences.

*STATEMENT: Escalating Digital Censorship in India*

*New Delhi, February 28, 2026*

The Internet Freedom Foundation (IFF) is concerned by a cluster of online blocking and takedown actions and ISP level service disruptions reported between 24–28 February 2026. Across these incidents, users and affected services face restrictions without clear, timely reasons and without access to the underlying orders needed to challenge state action by exercising their rights to obtain legal remedy.

Developers reported severe, uneven disruption in access to Supabase across multiple Indian networks. Reporting indicates the disruption followed a government direction, with accounts suggesting use of Section 69A of the Information Technology Act, 2000. Yet there has been no public statement of the grounds, scope, or duration, and no accessible order for those impacted. Supabase has publicly stated that its domains became inaccessible due to a “ministry order”, and users have been pushed to workarounds such as alternative DNS or VPNs. In parallel, users on X (formerly Twitter) continue to receive “withheld in India” notices restricting specific posts within the country. Such notices usually do not provide the government order or its reasoning. Hence, for those who are being censored the basics of natural justice of a notice, opportunity for a hearing and remedy are delayed or absent.

This is enabled by secrecy built into the blocking framework. Section 69A is implemented through the 2009 Blocking Rules, which contemplate a committee process and, where feasible, notice to intermediaries and identifiable originators. But they also impose “strict confidentiality” over requests and actions taken. When orders and reasons are secret by default, affected persons cannot test legality, necessity, proportionality, or factual errors except through protracted litigation. When in _Shreya Singhal v. Union of India_ (2015), the Supreme Court upheld Section 69A while relying on the existence of procedural safeguards and reasoned decisions, indicating that impacted users could approach court in writ remedies. However, due to the operational secrecy and providing copies of orders and notices those who are censored and prevented from obtaining judicial remedy.

The February 2026 amendments to the IT Rules, 2021 further increase these risks. The substituted Rule 3(1)(d) requires intermediaries to remove or disable access within three hours of receiving “actual knowledge”, which can arise from a court order or a written “reasoned intimation” by authorised government officers. While the rule lists what a “reasoned intimation” should contain, the legal basis, statutory provision, nature of the unlawful act, and specific URL/identifier, the three-hour window pressures platforms to comply promptly which may often occur without any substantive assessment. These inherently opaque censorship practices are being accelerated through "Sahyog" portal. Developed by the Indian Cybercrime Coordination Centre (I4C), the Sahyog portal operates entirely without statutory footing, only being anchored in the IT Rules, 2021 that are created by executive notification. It functions as a censorship clearinghouse that deliberately bypasses the established, albeit weak, procedural safeguards of Section 69A. By routing automated takedown directives directly to intermediaries under Section 79(3)(b) of the IT Act, the portal structurally excludes citizens and impacted users from the grievance process.

We demand that the government introduce strictly judicially enforceable transparency requirements, publish all blocking orders, and restore the principles of natural justice to India's platform governance framework. Based on requests from our community we will also next week launch a rough public sheet in which social media users can input and add information on digital censorship.

"YouTube does not like free speech."

Let's dive into it.  
With real, verifiable data.

YouTube enforced COVID-19 medical "misinformation" rules.  
It also enforced an election integrity policy introduced in December 2020.  
That policy barred certain claims of widespread fraud in the 2020 U.S. presidential election.

These rules led to channel terminations and suspensions.  
Donald Trump’s channel was removed after January 6, 2021 and restored in March 2023.  
Sebastian Gorka was hit in 2021 over election claims.  
Children’s Health Defense was terminated in 2021 over vaccines.  
Dan Bongino faced action in 2022 over COVID content.  
Others followed through 2023 and 2024.

The election-fraud claims policy was retired in June 2023.  
The standalone COVID policy ended by December 2024.  
In 2025 Alphabet offered reinstatement for channels terminated under the retired rules.  
It also referenced prior Biden administration pressure on COVID content.  
Separate removals followed DOJ indictments and State Department sanctions.

Critics called the earlier enforcement viewpoint discrimination on political speech.  
YouTube called it policy compliance.  
No complete public list of affected channels exists.

This should show you how YouTube "free speech" works.  
They ban and remove under political pressure.  
Then they reinstate when the threat is gone.  
YouTube was transparent only after the risk disappeared.  
It did not push back while the pressures were still active.

That means if the pressure had remained persistent, YouTube would probably have kept banning and removing politically related content.  
No warnings.  
No transparency.

The Five Eyes (FVEY) intelligence-sharing alliance consists of five countries:

🇺🇸 United States
🇬🇧 United Kingdom
🇨🇦 Canada
🇦🇺 Australia
🇳🇿 New Zealand

It originated from intelligence cooperation between the UK and US during World War II and developed into the UKUSA Agreement, particularly focused on signals intelligence (SIGINT).

The five countries are sometimes described as having especially close intelligence-sharing arrangements, including cooperation between agencies such as the ..

NSA (US),  = National Security Agency
GCHQ (UK),  = Government Communications Headquarters
ASD (Australia), = Australian Signals Directorate
CSE (Canada), = Communications Security Establishment
GCSB (New Zealand).= GCSB = Government Communications Security Bureau

The important point is that Five Eyes is primarily an intelligence-sharing and security partnership — it is not itself a single database containing everybody's personal information.

WHAT THEY SHARE

1. Signals intelligence — communications and electronic intelligence

This is the original purpose of the alliance. 
The UKUSA agreement provides for cooperation involving:

communications intelligence
intercepted communications
technical intelligence
translation
analysis
code-breaking
intelligence assessments

The NSA and GCHQ explicitly describe the agreement as covering the sharing of communication, translation, analysis and code-breaking information. 
Australia, Canada and New Zealand subsequently joined.

Australia's partner agencies are:

🇦🇺 ASD — Australian Signals Directorate
🇺🇸 NSA — National Security Agency
🇬🇧 GCHQ — Government Communications Headquarters
🇨🇦 CSE — Communications Security Establishment
🇳🇿 GCSB — Government Communications Security Bureau

2. CYBERSECURITY INFORMATION
This is a very active area today.

In June 2026:
The Five Eyes cyber-security agencies jointly stated that sharing cyber-threat information is critical to their collective security. 
They specifically discussed rapidly evolving AI-related cyber threats.

That can include information about:

cyber attacks
malware
hacking techniques
vulnerabilities
hostile cyber actors
threat intelligence
attacks against critical infrastructure
emerging technologies and AI-related threats.

Australia's Home Affairs Department also says it works with Five Eyes partners on technology and data-security issues, including:

1: Telecommunications, 
2: AI, biotechnology, 
3: Quantum technology 
4: Data-classification/security standards.

3. LAW-ENFORCEMENT / CRIMINAL INFORMATION

This goes beyond traditional intelligence.

The Five Eyes countries cooperate on information concerning transnational crime, including:

-organised crime
-cybercrime
-child exploitation
-financial crime
-drugs
-border/security matters
-serious criminal activity.

Australia's Home Affairs Department specifically describes Five Eyes cooperation involving law enforcement, border protection and criminal justice information.

4. ENCRYPTED COMMUNICATIONS

This is particularly interesting.

The Five Eyes governments have publicly discussed obtaining lawful access to encrypted communications/data.

In their Statement of Principles on Access to Evidence and Encryption, they stated that governments may seek cooperation from technology companies to provide lawful access solutions. 
They also say access should be subject to authorisation, legal processes and oversight.

There is also a UK–US treaty, published in 2024, concerning access to electronic data for countering serious crime.

So there is absolutely a real government-to-government framework for obtaining and exchanging electronic information in certain circumstances.

BUT WHAT ABOUT DIGITAL ID?

The Australian Government's current Digital ID documentation says Australia's system is designed as a national system and says that, with consent, personal information is shared with participating providers/services. 
It also says no centralised database is created for the Digital ID itself.

The Digital ID Act does, however, provide mechanisms for information sharing concerning things such as Digital ID fraud and cybersecurity incidents within the Australian system.

So:

Digital ID ≠ Five Eyes intelligence database.

But Digital ID/cybersecurity systems can generate information that governments may lawfully access or share under Australian legislation and other international cooperation arrangements.

That's a much more accurate description.

WHAT ABOUT COVID?
This needs to be separated from the Five Eyes intelligence alliance.

YES:  During COVID, the Five Eyes governments did cooperate extensively on pandemic-related information.

There are several different kinds of cooperation that can get lumped together under the term "Five Eyes":

Intelligence cooperation
→ threats, foreign interference, hostile actors, security intelligence.
Health/pandemic cooperation
→ epidemiological information, emerging threats, research, border issues, public-health information and international coordination.
Cybersecurity cooperation
→ cyberattacks, hacking, infrastructure threats, malware, etc.
Law-enforcement cooperation
→ criminal investigations and information obtained under applicable legal processes.

Those are not necessarily the same databases or legal mechanisms.

THE PART THAT IS REALLY WORTH LOOKING AT
There is an important historical issue behind your question.
Five Eyes was originally built around signals intelligence — essentially intelligence obtained from communications and electronic signals.

The official NSA history says the UKUSA arrangement established policies and procedures for sharing communications intelligence and related information.

And Australia has legislation specifically governing the communication and retention of intelligence information concerning Australian persons by agencies such as ASD. 

The legislation requires rules governing that information and requires consideration of privacy protections.

So there are legal mechanisms under which information concerning Australians can be communicated, including internationally.

And there is another interesting development

The Five Eyes countries have their own intelligence oversight bodies that meet through the Five Eyes Intelligence Oversight and Review Council (FIORC). They exchange views and, where permitted, information about oversight and review practices.

So there are actually two sides to this:

INTELLIGENCE SHARING → Five Eyes agencies share intelligence.

OVERSIGHT → their independent oversight bodies also cooperate and compare practices.

Going one step further and investigate the specific connection between Five Eyes 
+ Australia's Digital ID Act 2024 
+ the Australian Privacy Act 
+ the Assistance and Access Act 
+ biometric data (face/fingerprint) 
+ whether information can legally be passed to the US/UK/Canada/NZ. 

That is where the question becomes much more specific and revealing.

There are genuine connections between Five Eyes cooperation, surveillance, cross-border data access and cybersecurity, but there is an important distinction: 
I found no evidence that Australia's Digital ID system automatically sends everyone's identity or biometric information into a Five Eyes database.

Here is what the law actually shows.
1. DIGITAL ID — WHAT CAN BE COLLECTED?

The Digital ID Act 2024 specifically regulates accredited Digital ID providers.

It places additional restrictions on:

-facial/biometric information
-unique identifiers
-sensitive personal attributes
-data profiling
-disclosure of personal information
-use of information for marketing
-law-enforcement access.

The Act expressly says that biometric information cannot simply be collected, used, disclosed or retained whenever a provider wants. Handling it generally has to fall within specific authorisations in sections 49 or 50.

The OAIC also specifically lists collection/retention of biometric information, unlawful disclosure to law enforcement and sharing identity information without express consent among matters that can generate a Digital ID privacy complaint.

BUT there are exceptions.
This is important.
The Act permits certain biometric handling in circumstances including:

-where authorised by a warrant;
-for specified identity/document purposes;
-for testing;
-for preventing/investigating Digital ID fraud;
-in certain cybersecurity circumstances.

And there are restrictions against using biometrics for one-to-many matching or determining whether somebody has multiple Digital IDs.

So I would not describe the Act as saying "the government cannot ever obtain your biometric information."

It doesn't say that.

2. CAN DIGITAL ID INFORMATION GO TO POLICE?

Yes, under specified circumstances.
The Digital ID Act contains a specific provision concerning enforcement.

Section 54 says an accredited entity generally cannot use or disclose personal information for enforcement-related activities unless specified conditions are satisfied.

One important exception involves a warrant.

There is also an exception relating to reporting suspected or actual:
-Digital ID fraud
-cybersecurity incidents.

And the OAIC actually conducted a privacy assessment of the ATO's myID system, specifically examining how enforcement agencies could request personal and biometric information. That assessment was published in August 2025.

So the statement:

"Police can never obtain Digital ID information"

would be incorrect.

But equally:

"Police automatically get everybody's Digital ID information"

would also be incorrect.

3. CAN THE INFORMATION GO OVERSEAS?

Yes — Australian privacy law does permit cross-border disclosure in certain circumstances.

This is one of the most important things I found.

Under Australian Privacy Principle 8 (APP 8), an Australian organisation generally has to take reasonable steps to ensure an overseas recipient doesn't breach the Australian Privacy Principles.

But there are exceptions.
The OAIC specifically identifies circumstances where personal information can be disclosed overseas:

A. The individual consents
There is an exception where the person is expressly informed of the consequences and gives consent.

B. Australian law requires or authorises it

This is much more significant.
APP 8.2(c) permits disclosure to an overseas recipient where the disclosure is:
required or authorised by Australian law or a court/tribunal order.

C. International information-sharing agreements

APP 8.2(e) allows an Australian government agency to disclose information where it is:
required or authorised under an international agreement relating to information sharing.

The OAIC says this can include treaties and certain formal written arrangements such as memoranda of understanding or official exchanges of letters.

D. Serious threats/criminal matters

There are also permitted situations involving things such as:

-serious threats to life, health or safety;
-serious unlawful activity;
-locating missing persons;
-diplomatic/consular functions.

So "Australian data can never leave Australia" is definitely not what Australian privacy law says.

4. WHAT ABOUT THE UNITED STATES?

This is where things get particularly interesting.

Australia and the United States have a formal Australia-US CLOUD Act/Data Access Agreement.

The Australian Government says it allows Australian law-enforcement and national-security agencies to obtain electronic information from US communications providers.

The reverse is also possible: US agencies can seek electronic data from Australian communications providers.
The types of providers potentially covered include companies providing:

-telecommunications
-messaging
-social media
-VOIP
-cloud/back-up storage
-other electronic communications services.

The government specifically gives examples such as Meta, Google and Twitter.

And the agreement can cover:
content data + traffic data + metadata.
That is a real, documented cross-border data-access arrangement.

5. DOES THIS MEAN THE US CAN JUST LOOK AT AUSTRALIANS' DATA?

No.

There are restrictions.

The Australian Government says the agreement prohibits the US from targeting Australian persons under the agreement, and Australia is similarly prohibited from targeting US persons.

There are also requirements to minimise the acquisition, retention and dissemination of information about the other country's citizens when information is incidentally obtained.

Requests must also satisfy specified requirements, including serious-crime thresholds and independent review/oversight.

So there are legal safeguards, but there is nevertheless a genuine mechanism for cross-border access to electronic data.

6. WHERE DOES FIVE EYES COME INTO THIS?

This is a separate but related layer.

The five countries are:

🇦🇺 Australia
🇺🇸 United States
🇬🇧 United Kingdom
🇨🇦 Canada
🇳🇿 New Zealand
They have extensive intelligence cooperation.

They also jointly issued a Five Eyes Statement of Principles on Access to Evidence and Encryption.

This is particularly relevant. The five governments expressly stated that technology providers can be required under applicable law to assist authorities with lawful access to data, including communications content.

So there is absolutely a documented Five Eyes interest in obtaining access to encrypted communications when legally authorised.

7. ASSISTANCE AND ACCESS ACT 2018 — AUSTRALIA

Australia also has its own powerful legislation.

The Telecommunications and Other Legislation Amendment (Assistance and Access) Act 2018 created mechanisms under which designated communications providers can be required to provide assistance to agencies including:

-ASIO
-ASIS
-ASD
interception agencies.

The legislation contains provisions concerning technical assistance and access to electronic information.
And it isn't limited to Australian criminal investigations.

The legislation includes circumstances concerning foreign criminal offences and assistance to enforcement of foreign criminal laws.
That's a genuine international dimension.

8. AND THEN THERE IS THE 2021 IDENTIFY & DISRUPT LEGISLATION

Australia subsequently introduced additional powers through the Surveillance Legislation Amendment (Identify and Disrupt) Act 2021.

Among other things, this created:

Account takeover warrants

Authorities can take control of online accounts in specified circumstances.

Data disruption warrants

Authorities can disrupt/delete data associated with serious criminal activity.

Network activity warrants

These can allow collection of intelligence relating to criminal networks operating online.

The Australian Government describes these powers as being aimed at serious online crime, including activity involving encrypted/anonymising technology.

9. DOES FIVE EYES SHARE BIOMETRIC DATABASES?

This is where I would be very careful.

I have found evidence of:

Five Eyes intelligence sharing
↓
 cross-border information sharing
↓
 law-enforcement cooperation
↓
 electronic-data access
↓
 cybersecurity cooperation
↓
 biometric systems being used by individual governments

10. WHAT ABOUT FACIAL RECOGNITION?

Facial recognition is definitely considered biometric information under Australian privacy law.
The OAIC specifically says biometric information can include:
-face
-fingerprints
-iris
-palm
-signature
-voice.
It also recognises facial-recognition and voice-print information as personal information.

Therefore, if a Digital ID provider obtains a facial biometric, that is not just ordinary identifying information.

It receives significantly stronger protection under the Digital ID Act.

11. THE BIG DISTINCTION YOU NEED TO KNOW

There are really three separate systems here:

SYSTEM 1 — DIGITAL ID
Identity verification.

Examples:
name → date of birth → documents → identity attributes → potentially biometrics

Governed by the Digital ID Act and Privacy Act.
SYSTEM 2 — LAW ENFORCEMENT / SURVEILLANCE

Examples:
phone → messages → metadata → IP addresses → cloud accounts → communications
Governed by legislation including the Telecommunications (Interception and Access) Act and Assistance and Access legislation.

SYSTEM 3 — FIVE EYES INTELLIGENCE

Examples:

foreign intelligence → signals intelligence → cyber threats → security intelligence → intelligence assessments

Shared between the five countries under intelligence arrangements.

12. BUT THEY CAN INTERSECT

It is also wrong to say: "Digital ID information can never be accessed or shared outside Australia."

Australian law expressly provides circumstances where personal information CAN BE DISCLOSED internationally, including under international information-sharing arrangements.

And Australia has separate arrangements that facilitate international access to electronic data, including the Australia-US CLOUD Act Agreement.

So there is a legal architecture allowing Australian information to cross borders, subject to the particular law, purpose, authorisation and safeguards involved.

🔴 ONE THING I WOULD NOT CLAIM WITHOUT EVIDENCE

I would not say: "If you get an Australian Digital ID, your biometric information automatically goes to America, the UK, Canada and New Zealand."
I cannot substantiate that from the legislation or official sources I checked.

What I can substantiate is considerably more nuanced:

Australian Digital ID → regulated identity information

Australian privacy law → permits specified overseas disclosures

Australian surveillance laws → permit specified access to electronic data

Australia-US CLOUD Act → facilitates direct cross-border electronic-data requests

Five Eyes → extensive intelligence/cybersecurity cooperation

Five Eyes governments → explicitly cooperate on lawful access to encrypted communications

Those are all documented.

And there is one particularly important document I'd suggest we examine next:

The actual Digital ID Act sections 44–55, especially sections 49, 50, 53 and 54, alongside the Privacy Act APP 6 and APP 8.

Those provisions show exactly when biometric information can be collected, when it can be disclosed, when law enforcement can obtain it, and when information can legally leave Australia.

If you want, I can go through those sections line-by-line in plain English and highlight the parts that could allow government/law-enforcement access to your information — including the exceptions that DONT require YOUR CONSENT.

text:
Sound the Alarm : IFF’s First Read on MeitY's Draft IT Rules Second Amendment, 2026

New Delhi, 30 March 2026

On 30 March 2026, the Ministry of Electronics and Information Technology published proposed amendments to the IT Rules, 2021, inviting public comments by 14 April,  a comment period of barely fifteen days for changes with far reaching consequences for free speech and intermediary governance in India. We have conducted a quick review of the draft amendments. Despite being presented as "clarificatory and procedural," they represent a dangerous expansion of executive power over online speech.

We wish to state at the outset that these proposed amendments need to be immediately withdrawn and every member in our citizenry should demand their roll back and stand with the Constitution of India. These proposed amendments come at a time of fear and increased government directed censorship, especially of online political speech that includes parody and satire of the government, including the Prime Minister.

In brief the five changes are listed below:

1. Rule 3(1)(g) and 3(1)(h): Insertion of phrases within existing clauses making data retention obligations under the IT Rules additional to retention requirements under any other law.

2. Rule 3(4): Insertion of a new clause that mandates intermediary compliance with MeitY-issued clarifications, advisories, directions, SOPs, codes of practice, and guidelines, making such compliance a condition for retaining safe harbour under Section 79 of the IT Act. These are not anchored to the rule making powers of the IT Act, 2000 and provide uncanalised power to MEITY despite it stating otherwise.

3. Rule 8(1) proviso: A substitution in the proviso that expands applicability of MIB’s oversight mechanism in Part III of the rules to:  (1) intermediaries and (2) users who are not “publishers” and post/share news and current affairs content online. This oversight mechanism contains the blocking powers of MIB by way of Rule 14 (Inter-Departmental Committee), Rule 15 (Procedure for issuing directions to block), and Rule 16 (Emergency blocking provisions).

4. Rule 14(2) : A substitution that expands the scope of the IDC from hearing "complaints or grievances" to hearing "matters", including those referred by the Ministry of Information and Broadcasting.

5. Rule 14(5) : Replaces "complaints or grievances" with "the matter" in relation to IDC examination and recommendations.

A massive expansion of an unconstitutional censorship and regulatory power

First and most concerningly, Rule 3(4) creates a sweeping power for MeitY to issue binding instruments which are not anchored in law such as clarifications, advisories, directions, SOPs, codes of practice, and guidelines that intermediaries must comply with as a condition of safe harbour under Section 79 of the IT Act.

The Supreme Court's 2015 judgment in Shreya Singhal v. Union of India (2015) 5 SCC 1, remains the foundational precedent governing intermediary liability. It constrains the proposed amendments in several ways. First, the court read down Section 79(3)(b) to require that "actual knowledge" of unlawful content must come through a court order or government notification. Any Rule 3(4) making MeitY, "clarifications, advisories, directions, SOPs", lower the constitutional threshold for intermediary due diligence obligations.

Further, the settled principle in Indian administrative law, reaffirmed in Indian Express Newspapers v. Union of India (1985) 1 SCC 641 and Confederation of Ex-Servicemen Associations v. Union of India (2006) 8 SCC 399, is that delegated legislation must remain within the four corners of the parent statute.  It is important to note that the rule-making power under Section 87(1) of the IT Act is confined to, "carry[ing] out the provisions" of the Act. Section 87(2)(zg) authorizes rules for intermediary guidelines under Section 79(2), and Section 87(2)(z) for blocking procedures under Section 69A(2). Justice Chandurkar's judgement in the Kunal Kamra case clearly found the FCU amendment was not properly referable to either provision. Hence, any Rule 3(4) mandating compliance with MeitY advisories would face identical challenges since they create substantive new obligations not contemplated by Sections 79 or 87.

Even though Rule 3(4)(b)(ii) states that such, “advisories” etc. need to, “clearly specify the statutory provision or legal basis under which it is issued”, since these are not required to be published or made public there is every likelihood these will be issued with secrecy and hence may just in a tautological manner refer back to Section 79(3)(b) of the IT Act. This is similar to a logical fallacy in which it is clearly observable that a student is cheating on an exam who then claims that they may be permitted to continue cheating since they are stating at the same time they are not cheating. 

The practical effect of Rule 3(4) is that intermediaries face a perpetual compliance threat. Any failure to comply with any MeitY-issued instrument, however vague, however rapidly issued may cost them their safe harbour. The response for an intermediary is over-compliance and over-censorship.

Circumventing existing stay orders

The original proviso to Rule 8(1) stated that Part III applied to intermediaries only "for the purposes of rules 15 and 16"  i.e., content blocking directions and emergency blocking. The amended proviso now extends this to Rule 14, bringing intermediaries and user-generated news/current affairs content under the jurisdiction of the Inter-Departmental Committee.

Under Rules 9(1) and 9(3) of the 2021 IT Rules, there is a Code of Ethics compliance requirement and the three-tier grievance redressal mechanism, both of which were stayed by the Bombay High Court on 14 August 2021 as prima facie violative of Article 19(1)(a) and ultra vires the IT Act. On the oversight mechanism in Rules 14, 15, and 16, the Bombay High Court granted the petitioners to seek relief on this rule when an Inter Departmental Committee is established. The Madras High Court affirmed this stay as having pan-India effect in its order of 16 September 2021 in T.M. Krishna v. Union of India, observing that "an oversight mechanism to control the media by the government may rob the media of its independence." 

Both these cases, along with other cases challenging various provisions of the 2021 IT Rules, are now pending adjudication before the Delhi High Court.

The expansion of Rule 8(1) to cover Rules 14, 15, and 16 is an attempt to expand the blocking powers of MIB to both intermediaries and users who are not “publishers” but post news and current affairs content online. The IDC can now examine "matters" relating to user-generated news content on intermediary platforms without the Code of Ethics framework having been adjudicated as constitutional; the government effectively obtains the content oversight machinery that three High Courts found illegal, through a different procedural door.

Transforming the IDC from Grievance Body to Censorship Apparatus

The original Rule 14(2) required the IDC to hear "complaints regarding violation or contravention of the Code of Ethics." The amended version removes this requirement entirely. 

The IDC now hears:
(a) grievances arising from decisions at Level I or II; or
(b) "matters" referred to by the Ministry.

Clause (b) is unconstrained since, (a) there is no requirement that the "matter" arise from a complaint, (b) no requirement that the "matter" relate to a Code of Ethics violation; and (c) no requirement that the affected party be heard before the referral. The Ministry of Information and Broadcasting can, on its own motion, refer any content-related "matter" to the IDC. 

The cumulative effect of the amendments to Rules 8 and 14 is to reconstruct the oversight machinery that the Bombay and Madras High Courts found constitutionally suspect, in a form designed to evade the existing interim orders. The IDC, previously limited to the three-tier complaints process under the stayed Rules 9(3), 12, and 13 framework, now operates as a free-standing censorship committee that can take up "matters" referred by the executive.

Increased user surveillance through mandatory data retention directions

Insertion of phrases within existing clauses making data retention obligations under the IT Rules additional to retention requirements under any other law. For instance, the mandatory data retention of user data beyond 180 days within Rule 3(1)(g) and 3(1)(h) may be prescribed for longer periods and other purposes raising risks of surveillance and even potentially data leaks of sensitive data that is stored for longer periods of time. Government mandates for data retention as to their legal authority and hence period of retention will be beyond those contained under the IT Act.

SOS for Digital Rights 

IFF urges an urgent rollback!

We are alarmed by the continuing expansion of unchecked executive power that is opposed to the Constitution of India. The present actions of MEITY smack of digital authoritarianism and we call on them to withdraw these proposed amendments. 

The proper course is to await judicial determination of the pending challenges, respect interim protections granted by constitutional courts, and pursue regulatory objectives through parliamentary legislation rather than subordinate instruments that exceed the parent statute.

If not withdrawn, IFF will file a detailed response before the comment deadline. We call upon all stakeholders to submit their objections before 14 April 2026 at itrules.consultation@meity.gov.in

text:
Prof. Manoj Kumar Jha @manojkjhadu, your “Muffled Voices” poses a question India cannot afford to answer casually: what if democracy survives electorally, yet citizens gradually become afraid to speak? 

More unsettling still—what if nobody formally silences us because anticipated consequences teach us to silence ourselves?

🧵 FREEDOM OF EXPRESSION & DEMOCRACY’S FATE: THE CONSTITUTIONAL ANATOMY OF A “CHILLING EFFECT”

You begin where democracy actually begins—not with elections, but information.

Alexander Meiklejohn's democratic theory treated speech as indispensable to self-government: citizens cannot meaningfully govern unless they can hear, question and judge competing claims.

India constitutionalises that intuition through Article 19(1)(a).

But freedom is deliberately not absolute. Article 19(2) permits reasonable restrictions concerning sovereignty and integrity of India, State security, friendly relations with foreign States, public order, decency or morality, contempt of court, defamation and incitement to an offence.

The constitutional equation is therefore neither:

Speech > everything

nor

State > speech

but:

Liberty + narrowly justified restraint = constitutional democracy.

The Supreme Court has repeatedly stressed that restrictions cannot simply be invented beyond Article 19(2)'s enumerated grounds.

text:
India already possesses a constitutional compass.

Romesh Thappar (1950) located circulation of ideas near democracy's foundations.

Bennett Coleman (1972) protected press freedom against measures whose practical effect constrained circulation.

Indian Express Newspapers (1985) reaffirmed press freedom within Article 19(1)(a).

Shreya Singhal (2015) struck down IT Act Section 66A, powerfully distinguishing discussion, advocacy and incitement.

Subramanian Swamy (2016) nevertheless upheld criminal defamation—reminding absolutists that reputation also receives constitutional protection.

Anuradha Bhasin (2020) reaffirmed press freedom and subjected restrictions affecting internet-based expression to constitutional scrutiny, while discussing chilling effect.

The jurisprudential message is beautifully difficult:

Protect dissent without constitutionalising abuse; regulate harm without bureaucratising truth.

Your @manojkjhadu concern over governmental “fact-checking” acquires special contemporary significance.

The Bombay High Court struck down the 2023 IT Rules amendment enabling a Central Government Fact Check Unit concerning information about Central Government business, finding constitutional defects including vagueness and restrictions beyond Article 19(2).

But the story is not finished.

As of 20 August 2026, the Union's appeal is alive before the Supreme Court. 

In March 2026, the Court issued notice, declined to stay the Bombay High Court judgment and indicated that significant constitutional questions concerning misinformation require consideration.

That makes Jha's question remarkably current:

Can Government legitimately combat misinformation concerning itself without becoming simultaneously interested party, complainant and arbiter of truth?

Equally:

Can constitutional democracy simply abandon the information ecosystem to commercially incentivised misinformation?

Neither extreme solves the problem.

Independent process, statutory precision, transparency, proportionality and judicial review offer the more defensible middle path.

April 4, 2026 | New Delhi: The Editors Guild of India is deeply concerned by both the contents and the underlying intent behind the Draft Information Technology (Intermediary Guidelines and Digital Media Ethics Code) Second Amendment Rules, 2026 (“Draft Amendments”), which were made public by the Ministry of Electronics and Information Technology (MeitY) on March 30, 2026, with just a fortnight given for comments.
Prima facie, the amended rules and guidelines, whose stated purpose is to “strengthen compliance” and increase the effectiveness of regulatory oversight of content regulation mechanisms under Part III (Code of Ethics relating to Digital Media) of the IT Rules, 2021” appear to arm MeitY with sweeping powers of content regulation, sharply increases the compliance burden on digital intermediaries, and gives the executive overarching powers to block or take down content generated by  “non news publishers” and intermediaries. This will directly infringe the fundamental right to free speech guaranteed to all citizens under the Constitution and will have a chilling effect on freedom of expression and the airing of contrarian views, which are fundamental to an open and functional democracy.
Sub-rule (4) to Rule 3, which deals with due diligence obligations of intermediaries, now makes it mandatory on the part of intermediaries to comply with “any clarification, advisory, order, direction, standard operating procedure, code of practice or guideline issued by the ministry, by order in writing”. Failure to comply has been linked to loss of the safe harbour protection extended to intermediaries and platforms for user-generated content, under section 79 of the Information Technology Act. The absence of due process for the issuance of compliance orders and the complete lack of transparency in the process are deeply concerning.
Changes to Rule 14(2) and Rule 14(5) in the draft amendment also greatly widen the powers of the Inter-Departmental Committee (IDC). IDC, a central oversight body constituted under Rule 14 of the Information Technology (Intermediary Guidelines and Digital Media Ethics Code) Rules, 2021, was specifically created to hear grievances and complaints against digital content. Now, the IDC has been empowered to deal with and “matter” – a generalisation which arms the body to consider virtually any issue, in the absence of any definition of what constitutes a “matter”. Other provisions devolve rulemaking powers entirely to the executive branch, removing the window for legislative oversight provided under the IT Act.
The EGi calls on the government to urgently review or recall the draft rules, and engage in more constructive consultations with all sections of stakeholders and take on board valid concerns and objections.
Warm regards,
Sanjay Kapoor, President
Raghavan Srinivasan, General Secretary
Teresa Rehman, Treasurer

🛑 LEGAL NOTICE

To,  

Mr. Kunal Kamra
Comedian
X Handle: @kunalkamra88

Subject: Legal Notice for Immediate Removal of Derogatory Video, Public Apology, and Cessation of Further Acts Outraging Hindu Religious Sentiments, Failing Which Legal Proceedings Shall Be Initiated.

Mr. Kunal,

1. You have, on or around 15 July 2026, during a protest/event organised by the “Cockroach Janta Party” at Jantar Mantar, Delhi, made and circulated a highly offensive, derogatory, and blasphemous statement in a video speech. 

2. In the said video (also uploaded/covered by HNP News at https://t.co/mdQV2ex1dP), you deliberately uttered words to the effect: “Sita ke pati ka naam le lekar Nita ke pati ka kaam kar rahe hain” (and elaborated in a similar mocking and irreverent tone). 

3. Here, “Sita ke pati” refers to Bhagwan Shri Ram and is used in conjunction with “Nita ke pati” (referring to a corporate figure). You thereby reduce the sacred names and divine personas of Bhagwan Shri Ram and Maa Sita, revered Deities central to Hindu faith, Dharma, and the religious beliefs of millions of Hindus, to mere tools for crude political commentary and sensationalism. 

4. The tone, context, and delivery clearly demonstrate mockery and contempt. Screenshots of the video are annexed for your reference.

Did Meta Make A Big Mistake By Removing PM Modi's Video??
- Amit Dubey

Meta did make a major error by temporarily removing Prime Minister Narendra Modi’s Facebook video, a move that sparked intense governmental backlash and severe legal warnings in India. In an interview on the channel of popular digital creator RJRaunac, cyber security expert Amit Dubey highlighted how this incident exposed deep flaws in how big tech operates.

PM Modi posted a video on July 23 addressing Gen Z students about the NEET paper leak controversy. The video was suddenly blocked and remained unavailable on Facebook for over five hours.

Meta initially cited legal obligations, but later blamed an automated AI filter glitch for the accidental takedown.

The Indian government and a parliamentary IT panel, led by MP Nishikant Dubey, heavily grilled Meta's global team. They rejected the "technical glitch" excuse, raising questions about potential algorithmic bias and systemic flaws.

Loss of Safe Harbour Protection: The Parliamentary Committee warned Meta that it could lose its "safe harbour" immunity under Section 79 of the IT Act if accountability isn't met. This protection shields Meta from legal liability for user-generated content; losing it would expose the company to massive legal vulnerabilities.

Demand for Zuckerberg's Apology: While Meta's Global Affairs chief Joel Kaplan conveyed an official apology to IT Minister Ashwini Vaishnaw, the parliamentary panel has heavily pushed for a personal, written apology from Meta CEO Mark Zuckerberg.

The incident has significantly damaged Meta’s standing in India its largest global user market reigniting intense national debates around digital sovereignty and the lack of human transparency in big-tech content moderation.
